title: How to edit these notes
text:
删除一篇笔记

删除对应的 .qmd 文件。
打开项目根目录的 _quarto.yml。
在 sidebar 的 contents 中删掉指向该文件的两行，例如：

- href: "etale morphism/definitions-and-intuitions.qmd"
  text: Definitions and Intuitions
如果只删除文件而不修改 _quarto.yml，网站构建时会提示找不到页面。

title: How to edit these notes
text:
新增一篇笔记
最简单的方法是复制一篇现有的 .qmd 文件，改名并修改内容，然后在 _quarto.yml 的对应章节加入：
- href: "etale morphism/examples.qmd"
  text: Examples
以后添加新的大主题时，可以新建一个文件夹，再在 _quarto.yml 中增加一个 section。文件夹名称最好使用小写英文和连字符，例如 perfectoid-spaces。






Tip最省事的工作方式



你也可以只负责写内容，然后告诉我“把这篇笔记放到某个章节并发布”。目录、链接、渲染和推送都可以交给我处理。

title: Definitions
text:
NoteNote



We will list some important equivalent definitions of étale morphisms and leave the discussion of their equivalence for later.

title: Definitions
text:
Equivalent definitions

Definition 1 A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is étale if it is

locally of finite presentation,
flat, and
unramified.



Definition 2 A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between varieties over \(k\) is étale if it induces isomorphisms on the tangent spaces at all points of \(X\).


Definition 3 A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is étale if it is smooth of relative dimension \(0\).


Remark 1. The second definition tells us that we can think of an étale map as a map that is locally an isomorphism. And for the definitions of the flat, unramified and smooth morphisms, see later.

title: Definitions
text:
Examples

Example 1 (open immersion) Every open immersion \(U\hookrightarrow X\) is étale. Nothing changes near a point of \(U\): we have only restricted our attention to a smaller open subset.


Example 2 Assume that \(n\) is invertible in the base field. On the punctured affine line, the map
\[
\mathbb G_m \longrightarrow \mathbb G_m, \qquad t\longmapsto t^n
\]
is étale. Infinitesimally, its derivative is \(nt^{n-1}\), which never vanishes on \(\mathbb G_m\).







WarningWhere the picture breaks



On the whole affine line, \(t\mapsto t^n\) ramifies at \(t=0\). The map is no longer étale there: the branches collide.

title: Smooth Morphisms
text: A smooth morphism is the relative version of a nonsingular variety. Roughly, its fibers are smooth and fit together uniformly over the base.

title: Smooth Morphisms
text:
Defitions

Definition 1 (standard smooth morphism) The projection
\[
\operatorname{Spec}(R[x_1,\cdot, \cdot, x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\cdot, f_r)) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(R)
\]
is called the standard smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n\) if the determinant of the matrix
\[
\left(\frac{\partial f_i}{\partial x_j}\right)_{1\leq i,j\leq r}
\]
is invertible in the ring \(R[x_1,\cdot, \cdot, x_{n+r}]/(f_1,\cdot, f_r)\).


Remark 1. The fibers of this morphism are smooth varieties of dimension \(n\) by the Jacobian criterion. The condition on the determinant is a relative version of the Jacobian criterion.


Definition 2 (smooth morphism) A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is smooth of relative dimension \(n\) if there exist open coverings \(\{U_i\}\) of \(X\) and \(\{V_i\}\) of \(Y\) such that \(f(U_i)\subseteq V_i\) and for each \(i\), the restriction \(f|_{U_i}\colon U_i\to V_i\) is a standard smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n\).


Definition 3 (smooth variety) A variety \(X\) over a field \(k\) is smooth if the structure morphism \(X\to \operatorname{Spec}(k)\) is smooth.







Tip



Such definition for smooth variety is a little bit indirect, but it is convenient for our discussion since we will not spend much time on smooth varieties.

title: Smooth Morphisms
text:
Basic properties

Proposition 1 If \(f\colon X\to Y\) and \(g\colon Y\to Z\) are smooth morphisms of relative dimension \(n\) and \(m\) respectively, then the composition \(g\circ f\colon X\to Z\) is also smooth of relative dimension \(n+m\).


Proof. This is a local property, so we can assume that \(f\) and \(g\) are standard smooth morphisms of relative dimension \(n\) and \(m\) respectively. Then, by the chain rule, the corresponding Jacobian matrix of the composition \(g\circ f\) is a block-upper-triangular matrix with the Jacobian matrices of \(f\) and \(g\) on the diagonal. Therefore, the determinant of the corresponding square matrix of \(g\circ f\) is the product of determinants of the square matrices of \(f\) and \(g\), which are both invertible. So \(g\circ f\) is a standard smooth morphism of relative dimension \(n+m\).


Relation to differentials
We recall the definition and properties of the sheaf of differentials in Unramified Morphisms. The sheaf of differentials can be used to characterize smooth morphisms and smooth varieties.

Proposition 2 A variety \(X\) over \(k\) is smooth if and only if the sheaf of differentials \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is locally free of rank \(\dim(X)\).


Proof. When \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is locally free of rank \(\dim(X)\), we know that the Jacobian matrix has full rank at every point, which implies that \(X\) is smooth. Conversely, assume \(X\) is smooth. Then, by the relation between smoothness and regualrness, one can show that \(X\) is reduced. Since \(X\) is of finite type, the sheaf of differentials \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is of finite type. By the relation between the cotangent space and the fibre of the sheaf of differentials, we have \(\dim_{k(x)}(\Omega_{X/k}\otimes k(x))=\dim(X)\) for all closed points \(x\in X\). Therefore, we conclude that \(\Omega_{X/k}\) is locally free of rank \(\dim(X)\).







CautionCaution



It is not easy to show that a smooth variety is reduced. The proof is not included here, but it can be found in the textbook “The Rising Sea”. And the last statement in the proof above is a corollary of Nakayama’s lemma, which is a fundamental result in alegbraic geometry, and both reducedness, finiteness and the constantness of the dimension of fibre matter. See 14.3.J in “The Rising Sea” for details.


:::{#prp-smooth-and transitive-exact-sequence name=““} Let \(f\colon X\to Y\) and \(g\colon Y\to Z\) be morphisms of schemes. If \(f\) and \(g\) are smooth, then the transitive exact sequence is exact on the left, too, which means that the sequence \[
0\to f^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\to \Omega_{X/Z}\to \Omega_{X/Y}\to 0
\]
is exact. :::

Proof. This is a local property, so we can assume that \(f\) and \(g\) are standard smooth morphisms of relative dimension \(n\) and \(m\) respectively. Then, by ?@lem-derivation-of-polynomial-ring, we know the module of differentials is the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix. The injectivity of the left follows from the fact that the Jacobian matrix of \(g\circ f\) is a block-upper-triangular matrix with the Jacobian matrices of \(f\) and \(g\) on the diagonal.

title: Unramified Morphisms
text: To study unramified morphisms, we need to understand the sheaf of differentials first.

title: Unramified Morphisms
section: Definition of the sheaf of differentials
text:
Definition of the sheaf of differentials
For schemes \(X\) over \(Y\), there is a quasicoherent sheaf, \(\Omega_{X/Y}\), on \(X\). We call it the sheaf of differentials.

Definition 1 (sheaf of differentials) The sheaf \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is globally defined as the quotient \(\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2\), where the ideal sheaf \(\mathscr I\) is the sheaf of ideals defining the diagonal embedding \(X\to X\times_Y X\). One can check that \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is indeed a sheaf on \(X\). We define a map \(d\colon \mathscr O_X\to \Omega_{X/Y}\) by \(d(f)=\operatorname{pr}_1^*f-\operatorname{pr}_2^*f\) for \(f\in \mathscr O_X\).


Proposition 1 Affine locally, if \(X=\operatorname{Spec}(A)\) and \(Y=\operatorname{Spec}(B)\), then \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is the sheaf associated to the \(A\)-module \(\Omega_{A/B}\), which is generated by symbols \(da\) for \(a\in A\) subject to the relations: 1. \(d(a+a')=da+da'\) for all \(a,a'\in A\), 2. \(d(aa')=a\,da'+a'\,da\) for all \(a,a'\in A\), and 3. \(db=0\) for all \(b\in B\).


Proof. By definition, \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is the sheaf associated to the \(A\)-module \(I/I^2\), where \(I\) is the kernel of the morphism \(A\otimes_B A\to A\). It is generated by elements of the form \(a\otimes 1-1\otimes a\) for \(a\in A\). One can check that the map \(\Omega_{A/B}\xrightarrow I/ I^2\) given by \(da\mapsto a\otimes 1-1\otimes a\) is an isomorphism of \(A\)-modules.


Remark 1 (the universal property). The module \(\Omega_{A/B}\) is universal for \(B\)-derivations from \(A\) to an \(A\)-module \(M\). We skip the proof here, but one can find it in any standard textbook on algebraic geometry.

title: Unramified Morphisms
text:
Basic properties of \(\Omega_{X/Y}\)
There are two standard exact sequences of sheaves of differentials. The first one is the transitivity sequence: for morphisms \(f:X\to Y\) and \(g:Y\to Z\), there is an exact sequence \[
f^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Y}\longrightarrow 0.
\]
The second one is the conormal sequence: for a closed immersion \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) with ideal sheaf \(\mathscr I\), there is an exact sequence \[
\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2\longrightarrow i^*\Omega_{Y/Z}\longrightarrow \Omega_{X/Z}\longrightarrow 0.
\]






NoteConormal sheaf



We call \(\mathscr I/\mathscr I^2\) the conormal sheaf of \(X\) in \(Y\). It is a vector bundle on \(X\) if \(i:X\hookrightarrow Y\) is a regular immersion.


The sheaf of differentials \(\Omega_{X/Y}\) is compatible with base change: for a cartesian diagram \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
X' & \xrightarrow{\mu} & X \\
\downarrow & {\square}\,& \downarrow \\
Y' & \longrightarrow & Y
\end{array}
\] we have a canonical isomorphism \[
\Omega_{X'/Y'}\cong \mu^*\Omega_{X/Y}.
\]
All these properties can be done by using Proposition 1 and the corresponding properties of \(\Omega_{A/B}\).






TipHint



For the two exact sequences, one can check the right one is indeed the cokernel. For the base change property, one can use the universal property of \(\Omega_{A/B}\).


Here is a property for \(\Omega_{A/B}\). For a localization \(S^{-1}A\) of \(A\), we have a canonical isomorphism \[
\Omega_{S^{-1}A/B}\cong S^{-1}\Omega_{A/B}.
\] One can check this using the universal properties of the module of differentials and localization, or using the explicit description of \(\Omega_{A/B}\) in Proposition 1.

title: Unramified Morphisms
text:
Easy calculations of some \(\Omega_{A/B}\)

A useful lemma

Lemma 1 Let \(B\) be a ring and \(A=B[x_1,x_2, \cdots]/(r_1, r_2, \cdots)\) be the ring over \(B\). Then \(\Omega_{A/B}\) is a free \(A\)-module generated by \(dx_1, dx_2, \cdots\) modulo the relations \(dr_1, dr_2, \cdots\).


Proof. For the convenience of the proof, we assume that \(A=B[x_1, x_2, \cdots]\). The general case can be reduced to this case by using the transitivity sequence. Let \(M=\oplus_i A\,e_i\) be the free \(A\)-module generated by \(e_1, e_2, \cdots\). We define a map \(\phi\colon M\to \Omega_{A/B}\) by sending \(e_i\) to \(dx_i\) in \(\Omega_{A/B}\). One can check that \(\phi\) is surjective. To show that \(\phi\) is injective, we construct an inverse map \(\psi\colon \Omega_{A/B}\to M\). For any \(a\in A\), we can write it as a polynomial in \(x_1, x_2, \cdots,x_n\). We define \(\psi(da)\) to be the formal differential of this polynomial. One can check that \(\psi\) is well-defined and is indeed the inverse of \(\phi\).



Differentials for field extensions

Lemma 2 Let \(L/K\) be a separable field extension. Then \(\Omega_{L/K}=0\).


Proof. For any \(\alpha\in L\), there exists a polynomial \(f\in K[x]\) such that \(f(\alpha)=0\) and \(f'(\alpha)\neq 0\). Then \(f'(\alpha)d\alpha=df(\alpha)=0\), which implies \(d\alpha=0\). Since \(\Omega_{L/K}\) is generated by \(d\alpha\) for \(\alpha\in L\), we have \(\Omega_{L/K}=0\).


Lemma 3 Let \(L/K\) be a purely inseparable field extension. Then \(\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0\).


Proof. Assume \(\text{char}(K)=p>0\). By the transitivity sequence and the structure of purely inseparable extensions, we may assume \(L=K[x]/(x^p-a)\) for some \(a\in K\). By Lemma 1, we have \(\Omega_{L/K}\cong L\,dx/(px^{p-1}\,dx)=L\,dx\neq 0\).


Lemma 4 If \(L/K\) is separably genrated by \(t_1,\cdots,t_n\in K\), then \(\Omega_{L/K}\) is a free \(L\)-module generated by \(dt_1,\cdots, dt_n\).


Proof. By Lemma 1 and localization, we have \[\Omega_{K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)/K}\cong K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\,dt_1\oplus\cdots\oplus K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\,dt_n.\]
By Lemma 2, we have \(\Omega_{L/K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)}=0\), which implies \(\Omega_{L/K}\cong L\,dt_1+\cdots+ L\,dt_n\) by the transitivity sequence. It remains to show that \(dt_1,\cdots, dt_n\) are linearly independent over \(L\). We will prove this by showing that there exist \(K\) derivations \(d_i\) such that \(d_i(t_j)=\delta_{ij}\). For any \(i\), we can extend the derivation \(\frac{\partial}{\partial t_i}\) on \(K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\) to a derivation \(d_i\) on \(L\) by using the fact that \(L/K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\) is separable. To be precise, if \(\alpha\in L\) is algebraic over \(K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)\), then there exists a polynomial \(f\in K(t_1,\cdots,t_n)[x]\) such that \(f(\alpha)=0\) and \(f'(\alpha)\neq 0\). We can define \(d_i(\alpha)\) to be the unique solution of the equation \(f'(\alpha)d_i(\alpha)+d_i(f)(\alpha)=0\). One can check that \(d_i\) is indeed a derivation on \(L\) and \(d_i(t_j)=\delta_{ij}\).



Differentials for normalization








Relation to the cotangent space

Lemma 5 Let \(X\) be a scheme over \(k\) and \(x\in X\) be a closed point with residue field \(\kappa (x)\) separable over \(k\). Then the cotangent space of \(X\) at \(x\) is isomorphic to \(\Omega_{X/k}\otimes \kappa(x)\).


Proof. Apply the conormal sequence to the closed immersion \(\operatorname{Spec}(k(x))\hookrightarrow X\), we have a map \(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2 \rightarrow \Omega_{X/k}\otimes \kappa(x)\), where \(\mathfrak m_x\) is the maximal ideal of \(\mathcal O_{X,x}\). We will show this surjection is actually a bijection. For convenience, let \(A=\mathcal O_{X,x}\) ,\(k'=\kappa(x)\) and \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_x\). Since the module of differentials is compatible with localization, it suffices to show that the map \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2 \rightarrow \Omega_{A/k}\otimes k'\) is a bijection. By Yoneda lemma, it suffices to show that for any \(k'\)-module \(M\), the map \[
\operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(\Omega_{A/k}\otimes k', M)\to \operatorname{Hom}_{k'}(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2, M)
\]
is a bijection. By the universal property of \(\Omega_{A/k}\), we have a bijection \(\operatorname{Hom}_{A}(\Omega_{A/k}, M)\cong \operatorname{Der}_k(A,M)\). By Lemma 2, we have \(\operatorname{Der}_k(k',M)=0\), which means that \[\operatorname{Der}_k(A,M)=\operatorname{Der}_{k'}(A,M)\cong \operatorname{Der}_{k'}(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2,M).\]
One checks that this is just the map defined above, and the last isomorphism will be shown when we discuss formally étale.







TipVariety case



In variety case, by Lemma 1, we could deduce that \(\mathfrak m_x/\mathfrak m_x^2\) and \(\Omega_{X/k}\otimes \kappa(x)\) both come from the cokernel of the Jacobian matrix. So they are isomorphic.

title: Unramified Morphisms
text:
Unramified morphisms

Definition 2 (unramified morphism) A morphism \(f\colon X\to Y\) between schemes is unramified if it is locally of finite type and \(\Omega_{X/Y}=0\).

By the transitivity sequence, unramified morphisms are stable under composition. By the base change property, unramified morphisms are stable under base change. One checks that unramified morphisms are also local on the target, so they are ``reasonable’’ in the sense of the textbook the rising sea.

Examples
By the above calculation of \(\Omega_{A/B}\), we have the following corollaries.

Corollary 1 If \(L/K\) is a field extension of finite type, then \(\operatorname{Spec}(L) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(K)\) is unramified if and only if \(L/K\) is a separable algebraic extension.


Proof. By Lemma 2, it suffices to show that if \(\operatorname{Spec}(L) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Spec}(K)\) is unramified then \(L/K\) is a separable algebraic extension.
If \(L/K\) is inseparable, then \(\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0\) by the transitive exact sequence and Lemma 3. Thus, \(L/K\) is separable. If \(L/K\) is trancendental, then \(\Omega_{L/K}\neq 0\) by Lemma 4. Therefore, the extension \(L/K\) must be algebraic separable.

title: Étale Morphisms
text:
NoteSite



“An étale morphism is the analogue in algebraic geometry of a local isomorphism of manifolds in differential geometry, a covering of Riemann surfaces with no branch points in complex analysis, and an unramiﬁed extension in algebraic number theory.”–Milne.


Since the author, I, hasn’t learned flat morphisms and unramified morphisms seriously yet, but already has a basic understanding of the étale site and étale cohomology, which means that the author is familiar to some basic properties of étale morphisms and use it. Our main goal in this chapter is to understand the various equivalent definitions of étale morphisms and to get some intuition for what they are analog to. One of the purpose of this chapter is to figure out which property of étale morphisms comes from the flatness and which property comes from the unramifiedness. The author will try to understand the definition of étale morphisms in a more intuitive way, and then try to understand the properties of étale morphisms from the perspective of flatness and unramifiedness.
For a first pass, continue to Definitions.
